blocks.text: She deals harshly with her young, as though they were not hers] The Chaldee renders it very differently: שיחנא על בניא דלא דילה, She warms children that are not hers, that is, another's eggs, from which chicks may emerge. The Syriac: ܐܣܓܝܬ, she multiplies children not her own. The Arabic follows the same, and this describes the habits of the ostrich very well; of it Damir says: متي وجدت بيضة نعامة اخري تحضنها وتنسي بيضها [matā wajadat bayḍat naʿāma ukhrā taḥḍunuhā wa-tansā bayḍahā], If she comes upon the eggs of another ostrich, she warms them and forgets her own. Yet the Hebrew does not admit this rendering. Pagninus has: He makes her forget her young, in which they will not be. This I do not understand. Junius: God, by heating, hatches her young by another's work; that is, by the heat of the sun He warms the eggs which the ostrich had laid in the sand, until the chicks are hatched, as he also says in his Notes. For since he saw that learned men affirmed this of the ostrich, he tried to bend the Hebrew text in that direction. But the simplest rendering is the one we have given, and therefore also the most ancient: She deals harshly with her young. In Hebrew הקשיח בניה. The verb הקשיח occurs only here and in these words of Esa. LXIII, 17. Why didst thou let us stray from thy ways, O Lord, and תקשיח לבנו מיראתך, harden our heart from thy fear? There the Septuagint has Ἐσκλήρυνας τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν [Esklērynas tas kardias hēmōn]; and Jerome, Thou hast hardened our heart? Nor do the Syriac and the Arabic differ. That is, קשח with Cheth is the same as הקשה with He, except that in the former the stronger aspiration seems to intensify the meaning. Thus in Arabic too قسي [qasā] means to be hard, but قسح [qasaḥa] to be very hard and to be rigid. Hence قساح [qassāḥ] hyena, because it has a stiff neck, in no way flexible. And رمح قاسح [rumḥ qāsiḥ] is a hard and rigid spear, like the spear of Lausus, of which the Poet speaks in the tenth book of the Aeneid:
He came up, and with rigid spear struck Dryops from afar.

Transferred, then, to the mind, قسح [qasaḥa] or קשח means to be hard and unbending of mind; and הקשיח either to be hardened or to deal harshly with someone ^{(3)}. Accordingly Jerome here has She was hardened toward her young. And Augustine: She hardened herself against her young. And the Greeks: Ἀπεσκλήρυνε τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς [Apesklēryne ta tekna autēs], that is, τὴν περὶ τὰ τέκνα φυσικὴν στοργήν [tēn peri ta tekna physikēn storgēn]: She hardened her natural affection toward her young, as Olympiodorus rightly explains. To this belong these words of Jeremiah, Thren. IV, 3: The daughter of my people is cruel, [II, 860] like the ostriches in the wilderness. And the fact that the ostrich is called חסמם in Hebrew and ظليم [ẓalīm] in Arabic, that is, impious, unjust, as we have shown above ^{c)}. That the verb הקשיח is used here in the masculine for the feminine will surprise only one who does not know how frequent this enallage of gender is in Hebrew, especially concerning animals. Thus Esa. XIV, 11. תחתיך יצע רמה ומכסיך תולעה, Beneath thee the worm is spread, and the maggot covers thee. There the nouns are feminine but the verbs masculine. Conversely, in Exod. VIII, 2. [var. 6.] ותעל הצפרדע, And the frog came up; and in verse 14 [var. 6], ותהי הכנים, And the louse was: feminine verbs are joined to masculine nouns. Kimchi, on Isaiah, says this is the custom of Scripture [col. 255] when it speaks not of this or that animal but על דרך כלל, universally, of the whole species, as here of the ostrich. Her young, in Hebrew בניה, her children, that is, the eggs from which chicks would have emerged had she warmed them. So they are called children δυνωτικῶς [dynōtikōs, potentially]. Like that line of Martial, book 9, Epigram 42:
What you waste with your fingers, Ponticus, is a man.

As though they were not hers] In Hebrew ללא לה. In full it would be כאשר לא יהיו לה. As in Iob. X, 19. כאשר לא הייתי, As though I had not been ^{(4)}. But in this book the style is sometimes very concise, because it is not prose but verse. And this antithesis has its own charm: her children, as though not hers. Like that of Paul, 1 Cor. VII, 30. Οἱ κλαίοντες ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες, καὶ οἱ χαίροντες ὡς μὴ χαίροντες [Hoi klaiontes hōs mē klaiontes, kai hoi chairontes hōs mē chairontes], etc. Those who weep as though not weeping, and those who rejoice as though not rejoicing, etc. And Hebr. XI, 27. Τὸν γὰρ ἀόρατον ὡς ὁρῶν [Ton gar aoraton hōs horōn]: As seeing him who is invisible.
